meta.descriptionEn: In October 1977, a hospital cook in the Somali port town of Merca agreed to guide two sick children through town in a closed Land Cruiser. The trip took no more than 15 minutes. It would make him the last known person on Earth to catch smallpox naturally. This documentary traces how a disease that was still causing around 2 million deaths a year in 1967 was driven to the edge of extinction, how a chain of mistakes almost let it slip through, and how 161 contacts were traced and 54,777 people vaccinated in just two weeks. Then follow Ali Maow Maalin into his second mission, fighting polio, and see what his story teaches us today.
meta.descriptionUr: Oktobar 1977 mein Somalia ke shehar Merca mein aik hospital cook ne do beemar bachon ko gaari mein le jane mein madad ki. articleEn: In October 1977, a closed Land Cruiser was driving along a road in the Somali coastal town of Merca. Inside were two sick children. With them was a 23-year-old named Ali Maow Maalin. Maalin worked as a hospital cook and sometimes served as a vaccinator alongside the WHO team. On this day his job was simply to show the way. It was a small task, but its consequences were enormous.

The trip lasted at most 5 to 15 minutes. It is believed he was infected during those few minutes. Within days he became someone the world still remembers: the last known person to catch naturally occurring smallpox.

This raises some big questions. How did humanity defeat such a frightening disease? How did a hospital cook become the last patient? And, biggest of all, since so many people had met him, how was an outbreak stopped from spreading?
This article tells the whole story, from ancient history to Jenner's vaccine and on to the final fight in Somalia. First, let us climb into that closed vehicle and see where the story began.

articleEn: Smallpox, called chechak in Urdu, was a disease caused by the variola virus, a member of the Orthopoxvirus family. Its traces in human history are very old. The earliest physical evidence comes from Egyptian mummies who died roughly 3,000 years ago. Genetic evidence suggests the virus probably emerged 3,000 to 4,000 years ago, and before that similar viruses probably lived only in other animals.

Several ancient epidemics raise questions. Some historians think the Plague of Athens in 430 BCE may have been smallpox. Galen's description of the Antonine Plague suggests it was probably smallpox too. It spread through the Roman Empire from 165 to 180 CE, and an estimated 5 million people died. Still, ancient records are not detailed enough to be certain. India's ancient text, the Sushruta Samhita, mentions a disease with pustules, and people there also imagined Sitala, a goddess of the illness. In 581 AD Gregory of Tours wrote the first reliable account of its symptoms in Western Europe. In the ninth century Rhazes distinguished it from measles and chickenpox. By the 18th century smallpox was among the major causes of death, killing about 400,000 Europeans each year, including 5 reigning monarchs.

How did the illness unfold? First came fever, headache, fatigue and nausea. Then spots appeared on the skin, and these turned into fluid-filled blisters. The first symptoms usually appeared 7 to 14 days after infection. The disease spread mostly through prolonged face-to-face contact. There was no evidence of spread by insects or animals, and there were no symptom-free carriers.

The most important point is that there were two main forms. Variola major was more severe and Variola minor was milder. Historically, about 30 percent of Variola major patients died, while Variola minor killed around 1 percent or fewer. Many survivors were left with permanent scars on the skin, and some lost their sight.

The numbers are still startling. The 735 to 737 epidemic in Japan is believed to have killed about a third of the population. In the 18th century, it is estimated that smallpox caused about a third of all blindness cases. Over thousands of years the disease reached Europe, Asia and Africa. The next question is what happened when it reached the Americas.

articleEn: Now the story crosses the Atlantic. Among the diseases that moved from the Old World to the New in the Columbian exchange was smallpox. Some believe that 90 to 95 percent of the native population of the New World was lost to Old World diseases, with smallpox a major cause.

In 1519 Hernán Cortés landed on the coast of what is now Mexico, then home to the Aztec Empire. In 1520 another Spanish group arrived from Hispaniola, bringing smallpox, which had already spread on that island for two years. One of Cortés's men caught it. When Cortés returned to Tenochtitlan, the disease went with him and the Aztecs revolted. The Spanish had to retreat, and Cortés did not return to the capital until August 1521. Meanwhile smallpox wiped out about 25 percent of the Aztec population.

The impact on the Inca Empire in the south was even deeper. Starting in Colombia, the disease spread before the Spanish arrived. Within months many leaders died, including Emperor Huayna Capac and his successor. A struggle for power broke out between two sons, and Atahualpa became the new emperor. In this weakened moment Francisco Pizarro arrived. It is believed that within a few years smallpox destroyed 60 to 90 percent of the Inca population.

Boston suffered six epidemics from 1636 to 1698. The worst came in 1721, and when people fled the city the virus reached the rest of the Thirteen Colonies. Much later, from 1901 to 1903, Boston recorded 1,596 cases. About 300 people died, a fatality rate of 17 percent.

The danger had not ended even in the 20th century. It is estimated that smallpox caused 250 to 500 million deaths in that century. Another source says the figure is at most 300 million, so estimates differ. Either way, the loss was huge. In the early 1950s there were about 50 million cases a year. In 1967, according to WHO, 15 million people fell ill and 2 million died. So even in 1967 the disease was a huge threat, and that year WHO stepped up its efforts to end it. But how was this done?

articleEn: The story starts with a very old observation: a person who had smallpox once did not get it again. From this idea came variolation, in which a healthy person was deliberately given a mild infection using material from smallpox sores. Our sources say variolation began in China in the 10th century, although the first written records appear around 1500, so the dates differ. In 17th-century India, Europeans observed a large needle being dipped in smallpox material and applied to the skin.

Then came Lady Mary Wortley Montagu. In 1713 her brother died of smallpox, and two years later she caught the disease herself. When her husband became ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, she went to Constantinople. There she saw variolation and wanted the same for her son. Charles Maitland carried out the procedure on her son, who came through safely. When an epidemic broke out in London, the same was done for her daughter, and the story reached the newspapers. Princess Caroline of Wales wanted more evidence for her own children, so trials were held on an orphanage and some convicts. After their success, royal approval followed.

There were problems, though. Variolation started local outbreaks, and two cases ended in death, so public reaction was harsh. Its popularity then declined somewhat. Robert and Daniel Sutton made it popular again. They made the method milder and proposed mass variolation of whole areas during an epidemic.

Now to Edward Jenner. He himself had been variolated in 1756 at the age of eight. On 14 May 1796, Jenner took material from a cowpox sore on the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes and applied it in small cuts on the arm of eight-year-old James Phipps. Phipps recovered. Two months later Jenner used smallpox material and saw no effect. Phipps thus became the first person to be immune without having had the disease.

Was Jenner the first? No. In 1774 a cattle dealer named Benjamin Jesty had inoculated his wife and three sons with cowpox. The difference was that Jenner was the first to prove the effectiveness of cowpox vaccination through scientific experiment. The Royal Society refused to publish Jenner's research, so in June 1798 he had his book printed in London, and it became a bestseller in elite circles. The word vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, meaning cow. Yet making a vaccine and wiping out a disease across the world were two very different tasks.

articleEn: Even after Jenner's vaccine, smallpox did not disappear at once. The real fight came in the 20th century, when WHO ran a worldwide vaccination campaign. According to one source, this global campaign ran from 1958 to 1977. It made smallpox the only human disease to be completely eradicated.

In endemic regions like Africa, a mass vaccination drive began in 1959, meaning vaccine was given to people on a large scale. This approach had very little success. Then, in the late 1960s, a more effective strategy emerged. Teams carried out active surveillance, going out themselves to look for cases. Wherever an outbreak was reported, rapid containment followed: people around the cases were vaccinated quickly and intensively. In 1967 WHO stepped up its efforts, and Donald Henderson led the eradication programme from 1967 to 1976.

Smallpox naturally infected only humans. It did not spread through insects or animals, and there was no symptom-free carrier. Remember also the two forms: Variola major with about 30% fatality and Variola minor with about 1% or less. The disease usually spread through close face-to-face contact, mostly after the rash appeared. That made finding and vaccinating contacts vital. Timing mattered too: if vaccine was given within three days of exposure, it often stopped the disease or reduced its severity. Also, immunity from the vaccine faded over time and probably ended within thirty years.

Results slowly appeared. By 1972 most African countries were free of smallpox. By the end of 1975 the virus had been eliminated from the whole world except the Horn of Africa. Smallpox remained in Ethiopia and Somalia, and in neighbouring Kenya. Why was it so hard in these three countries? One reason was the nomadic people of the Ogaden Desert, among whom endemic smallpox persisted. There the disease took an unusually mild form, which helped it survive in the population.

From 1975 WHO focused its efforts on this region. The last case in Ethiopia appeared in August 1976, and the last in Kenya in February 1977. So Somalia was now the hardest front. What was really going on there?

articleEn: Somalia lies in the Horn of Africa and shares a border with Ethiopia. The situation there was different because most of the population was nomadic. The country had about 3.5 million people, and reaching the nomads was quite difficult. A nationwide mass vaccination campaign in 1969 failed. Many nomads had cultural objections, so they refused or avoided it. In every campaign the biggest question is trust. When people avoid a vaccine, just sending teams is not enough. So elimination efforts there relied on an intensive reporting system, and getting information about cases was essential.

Then a severe drought struck in 1975. It increased movement of people across the border with Ethiopia, and outbreaks kept recurring. When people move more, the risk of spread also rises, and this was an extra challenge for the teams. In March 1977 surveillance found more than 3,000 cases in the south of the country, a sign of great danger. The Somali government declared a state of emergency and appealed to the United Nations for help, which succeeded. The campaign then began at full strength. By June, when the outbreak peaked, 3,000 Somali health workers and 23 international advisers were involved. It was a large effort: thousands of local workers, a few international experts, and one aim, to find and stop the last cases. Imagine a country with many nomads, and teams tracking them down to vaccinate them. It was not easy.

In July 1977 the Ogaden War began. It affected the eradication work because access to desert areas was limited. This was the setting in which another outbreak emerged in August 1977, in a nomadic group of twenty families. Between August and October, eight children in this group developed symptoms. This chain of events became a key turning point in our story.

On 12 October 1977, two children with smallpox symptoms were found at an encampment near Kurtunawarey, about 90 km from Merca. Local officers took the children by vehicle to Merca, where an isolation camp was nearby. Along as a guide was Ali Maow Maalin. Later, WHO workers brought this nomadic outbreak under control by 18 October. But one important link escaped their notice.

articleEn: Ali Maow Maalin was 23 at the time. He was a cook at the Merca hospital and sometimes acted as a vaccinator with the WHO smallpox team. Oddly, smallpox vaccination was compulsory for hospital staff, yet Maalin was not protected. Why? According to CDC epidemiologist Jason Weisfeld, Maalin had been vaccinated but it did not take. Other sources say he was never vaccinated. In a 2007 interview, Maalin himself said he had not been vaccinated. The reason was that he feared vaccination, because the shot seemed painful.

Now back to 12 October 1977. The two children with symptoms near Kurtunawarey had to be brought to Merca. Maalin served as guide on the trip. He was in a closed Land Cruiser with the children. According to sources, the vehicle went from the hospital either to the home of the surveillance supervisor or straight to the isolation camp. The trip lasted at most 5 to 15 minutes, yet it is believed that Maalin was infected in that short time. Among the children was a six-year-old girl, Habiba Nur Ali. She died two days later and is regarded as the last person to die of natural smallpox.

By 18 October the WHO team had contained the nomadic outbreak. But investigators did not identify Maalin as a contact. On 22 October Maalin developed fever and headache. At the hospital he was treated for malaria. Four days later a rash appeared on his skin. Probably assuming he had been vaccinated, he was thought to have chickenpox and was discharged from the hospital. Over the next few days the symptoms began to point to smallpox. But Maalin did not want to go into isolation, so he told no one himself.

During this time he was a popular man. According to Donald Henderson, relatives and friends kept visiting him during the illness, and he also moved around the hospital. On 30 October a nurse colleague reported him, reportedly perhaps because of a reward of 200 Somali shillings, roughly 35 dollars. Maalin was moved to the isolation camp. Based on symptoms, Variola minor was diagnosed, and laboratory tests later confirmed it. Consider this: a person who was part of the team fighting the disease had himself become the last natural case. The diagnosis date is written as 26 October 1977 in some places.

Maalin had no complications and recovered, leaving the camp at the end of November. Henderson called the case an example showing many weaknesses and mistakes in programme operations. The question now was how far the damage had spread.

articleEn: After Maalin went into isolation, the real test began. If any of his contacts had caught the disease, an outbreak could spread in Merca. Jason Weisfeld and Karl Markvart coordinated the response. The WHO team tracked down all of Maalin's contacts. They found 161 contacts, of whom 41 had not been vaccinated. Among them, 91 people had met Maalin face to face, and 12 of those 91 were unvaccinated. Some contacts lived up to 120 km from the town, so the search area was very wide. All contacts were kept under surveillance for six weeks. Face-to-face contacts and their families were vaccinated, and none showed signs of infection. Consider the effort: finding contacts, vaccinating them and watching them for six weeks demanded very organised work.

Merca Hospital was closed to new patients. All its medical staff were vaccinated, and the existing patients were quarantined there. Residents of fifty houses around Maalin's home were vaccinated, and the campaign was later extended to the whole ward where he lived. Then a house-to-house search was carried out across the whole town so that no new case stayed hidden. Police checkpoints were set up on every road out of the town, even on footpaths. Anyone found not recently vaccinated was vaccinated on the spot as they passed. It was like a protective wall around the town. In just two weeks after Maalin's isolation, 54,777 people were vaccinated, which shows how quickly and seriously WHO worked.

But the work did not end there. House-to-house searches continued every month in the region, and then a search across the whole of Somalia was completed in December 1977. On 17 April 1978 a telegram arrived from the WHO office in Nairobi: Search complete. No cases discovered. Ali Maow Maalin is the world's last known smallpox case. The containment in Merca had succeeded. None of Maalin's contacts fell ill, and the outbreak was stopped before it could begin.

But one last twist remained. In 1978 another smallpox outbreak came out of a laboratory in Birmingham, UK. Medical photographer Janet Parker was infected at the Birmingham Medical School and died on 11 September 1978. The source was laboratory virus. That is why Maalin is still regarded as the last case of naturally acquired smallpox: the Birmingham incident came from a laboratory, not from nature.
Finally, on 26 October 1979, two years after Maalin's rash, WHO declared global eradication of smallpox. Official certification followed in May 1980.

articleEn: How did Maalin's life go after smallpox? He stayed in the Merca area and did various jobs. In the mid-1990s he was selling medicines in a small nearby town. Then he became part of a new campaign, against poliomyelitis. Maalin was among the 10,000 volunteers who worked to rid Somalia of polio, an effort that succeeded in 2008. He explained his reason himself: Somalia had been the last country with smallpox, and he did not want it to be the last place for polio either.

He was a local coordinator for WHO, responsible for social mobilisation. For many years he travelled across Somalia vaccinating children and explaining things to communities. The Boston Globe counted him among WHO's most valuable local coordinators. When parents refused vaccines, he told them his story. He said he explained how important vaccines are and advised them not to make a foolish mistake like his.

Then in 2013 poliovirus returned to Somalia. Maalin was vaccinating in Merca district at the time when he developed a fever. A few days later, on 22 July 2013, he died of malaria. He stayed involved in vaccination work until the end.

Another question: has the smallpox virus been completely wiped out? No. Two live samples of variola major still exist, one at the US CDC in Atlanta and the other at Russia's Vector Institute. Research on them can only be done with the approval of WHO and the World Health Assembly. WHO proposed destroying the virus in 1986. The date was first set for 30 December 1993, then postponed to 30 June 1999. Because of opposition from the US and Russia, in 2002 the World Health Assembly allowed the stocks to be kept temporarily for specific research. Some scientists say the stocks may be useful for new vaccines, antiviral drugs and diagnostic tests, and the debate continues. But WHO-appointed experts said in 2010 that there is no essential public health reason to keep them. So who will decide, and when?

Maalin's story offers several lessons. If even one contact is missed, the danger can grow, which is why surveillance and contact tracing matter so much. The second lesson is that vaccination is not only a task but also a matter of trust. Maalin persuaded parents by telling his personal story. How do you think trust is built? shorts.titleEn: The 15-Minute Ride That Made Ali Maalin History
shorts.text: صرف 5 سے 15 منٹ کا سفر، اور ایک آدمی تاریخ میں امر ہو گیا۔ اکتوبر 1977 کی بات ہے۔ صومالیہ کے شہر Merca میں ایک بند Land Cruiser چل رہی تھی۔ اس میں smallpox کی علامات والے دو بچے تھے۔ ساتھ میں 23 سال کا ایک نوجوان تھا، Ali Maow Maalin۔ وہ ہسپتال میں cook تھا، اور کبھی کبھار WHO کی ٹیم کے ساتھ vaccinator بھی بنتا تھا۔ خیال ہے کہ اسی مختصر سفر میں وہ infect ہو گیا۔ بعد میں دنیا نے اسے ایک انوکھے نام سے یاد رکھا: قدرتی طور پر پھیلنے والی smallpox کا آخری معلوم مریض۔ تفتیش کرنے والوں نے بچوں کا outbreak 18 اکتوبر تک روک لیا، مگر Maalin کو contact کے طور پر پہچانا ہی نہیں۔ اس کے بعد کیا ہوا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Sirf 5 se 15 minute ka safar, aur ek aadmi tareekh mein amar ho gaya. Aktoobar 1977 ki baat hai. Somalia ke shehar Merca mein ek band Land Cruiser chal rahi thi. Is mein smallpox ki alamaat wale do bachay thay. Saath mein 23 saal ka ek naujawan tha, Ali Maow Maalin. Woh hospital mein cook tha, aur kabhi kabhar WHO ki team ke saath vaccinator bhi banta tha. Khayal hai ke isi mukhtasar safar mein woh infect ho gaya. Baad mein duniya ne use ek anokhay naam se yaad rakha: qudrati tor par phailne wali smallpox ka aakhri maloom mareez. Tafteesh karne walon ne bachon ka outbreak 18 October tak rok liya, magar Maalin ko contact ke tor par pehchana hi nahin. Iske baad kya hua? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: In October 1977, a hospital cook guided two sick children through Merca in a closed Land Cruiser. That short ride made him the last known person with naturally occurring smallpox.

shorts.titleEn: Why Did the Last Smallpox Patient Hide His Illness?
shorts.text: اگر کوئی بیمار شخص خود کو چھپا لے تو کیا ہوتا ہے؟ 22 اکتوبر 1977 کو Ali Maow Maalin کو بخار اور سر درد ہوا۔ چار دن بعد rash نکلا، مگر اسے chickenpox سمجھ کر discharge کر دیا گیا۔ حقیقت کیا تھی؟ CDC کے Jason Weisfeld کے مطابق vaccine لگی تھی مگر اثر نہیں کیا۔ دوسرے sources کہتے ہیں کہ لگی ہی نہیں تھی۔ 2007 کے interview میں Maalin نے خود بتایا کہ وہ vaccine سے ڈرتا تھا۔ پھر علامات smallpox کی طرف اشارہ کرنے لگیں، لیکن isolation کے ڈر سے اس نے خود اطلاع نہیں دی۔ 30 اکتوبر کو ایک nurse ساتھی نے اسے report کر دیا۔ شاید 200 Somali shillings کے انعام کے لیے۔ اب سوال یہ تھا کہ اس دوران وہ کتنے لوگوں سے مل چکا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Agar koi beemar shakhs khud ko chhupa le to kya hota hai? 22 October 1977 ko Ali Maow Maalin ko bukhar aur sar dard hua. Chaar din baad rash nikla, magar use chickenpox samajh kar discharge kar diya gaya. Haqeeqat kya thi? CDC ke Jason Weisfeld ke mutabiq vaccine lagi thi magar asar nahin kiya. Doosre sources kehte hain ke lagi hi nahin thi. 2007 ke interview mein Maalin ne khud bataya ke woh vaccine se darta tha. Phir alamaat smallpox ki taraf ishara karne lagin, lekin isolation ke dar se us ne khud ittila nahin di. 30 October ko ek nurse saathi ne use report kar diya. Shayad 200 Somali shillings ke inaam ke liye. Ab sawal yeh tha ke is dauran woh kitne logon se mil chuka tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: Ali Maow Maalin was discharged from hospital after being mistaken for a chickenpox case, and he did not report himself for fear of isolation. A colleague finally reported him on 30 October 1977.

shorts.titleEn: 54,777 Vaccinated in 2 Weeks: Stopping Smallpox in Merca
shorts.text: 54,777 لوگوں کو صرف دو ہفتوں میں vaccine لگی۔ وجہ کیا تھی؟ ایک ہی مریض: Ali Maow Maalin۔ WHO کی ٹیم نے اس کے سارے contacts ڈھونڈ نکالے۔ کل 161 contacts تھے، جن میں سے 41 کو vaccine نہیں لگی تھی۔ سب کو چھ ہفتے surveillance میں رکھا گیا۔ Merca Hospital نئے مریضوں کے لیے بند ہوا، اور اس کا سارا staff vaccinate ہوا۔ شہر سے نکلنے کے ہر راستے پر police checkpoints لگے، حتیٰ کہ footpaths پر بھی۔ پھر 17 اپریل 1978 کو WHO کے Nairobi office سے telegram آیا۔ اس میں لکھا تھا: Search complete. No cases discovered. مگر 1978 میں Birmingham کی ایک laboratory سے ایک اور outbreak نکلا۔ کیسے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: 54,777 logon ko sirf do hafton mein vaccine lagi. Wajah kya thi? Ek hi mareez: Ali Maow Maalin. WHO ki team ne us ke saare contacts dhoond nikale. Kul 161 contacts thay, jin mein se 41 ko vaccine nahin lagi thi. Sab ko chhe hafte surveillance mein rakha gaya. Merca Hospital naye mareezon ke liye band hua, aur us ka saara staff vaccinate hua. Shehar se nikalne ke har raste par police checkpoints lagay, hatta ke footpaths par bhi. Phir 17 April 1978 ko WHO ke Nairobi office se telegram aaya. Is mein likha tha: Search complete. No cases discovered. Magar 1978 mein Birmingham ki ek laboratory se ek aur outbreak nikla. Kaise? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: After Ali Maow Maalin was isolated, WHO teams traced 161 contacts and vaccinated 54,777 people in two weeks. On 17 April 1978 a telegram confirmed no further cases.
